events.title: IBM PC XT released
events.summary: [IBM] announced the Personal Computer XT in March 1983 — the first [IBM] [PC] with a built-in [hard disk] as standard equipment.
events.about: The XT's 10 MB hard drive and 8088 [CPU] made floppy-swap hell optional for business software. Clone makers copied its expansion slots and BIOS-compatible design, cementing the [PC] as the platform for [DOS] apps, early LANs, and eventually Windows. Internal storage became the default expectation for desktop development machines.

narrative.whyChosen: The [PC] XT normalized built-in [hard disk]s on [IBM]-compatible desktops.
narrative.whyImportant: It extended the open [PC] architecture that clone vendors and software houses built on.
narrative.problemSolved: Floppy-only PCs could not hold large databases, compilers, and multi-file projects comfortably.

events.title: Compaq Portable released
events.summary: Compaq Computer Corporation began shipping the Compaq Portable in March 1983 — the first [IBM] [PC]-compatible [portable computer].
events.about: Compaq legally reverse-engineered the [IBM] [PC] BIOS and shipped a luggable 8088 machine that ran unmodified [DOS] software — proving the [PC] standard could be cloned. The company grew into a server giant (later HP ProLiant). Every [PC]-compatible portable and white-box desktop traces legitimacy to this product.

narrative.whyChosen: The Compaq Portable was the first commercially successful [IBM] [PC] clone.
narrative.whyImportant: It established that [PC] compatibility could be replicated without [IBM]'s permission — opening the clone market.
narrative.problemSolved: Businesses wanted portable PCs that ran the same software as their [IBM] desktops.
